We believe and proclaim that the goodness of God will overcome the corrupt principalities and powers of this world, even if we do not live long enough to witness it. God’s goodness and justice will prevail. In Christ’s name it will be so! Hiraya Manawari!

We believe, proclaim, and echo the hope of the prophet Amos, that justice will come like a raging river sweeping away corruption and injustice from our land. We believe and trust that those who are responsible will be held accountable in some way or another.

Details of this will be announced further. Although this is an official church action and we encourage our members, leaders, and friends to attend, we also respect the personal conscience and autonomy of each one.
Open Table MCC, as a church, will join the protest rally against corruption this coming 21st of September, in Luneta Park, City of Manila.

Together with the ecumenical network and the sectoral justice movement, we denounce and condemn corruption in our country and those involved. The blood of every Filipino who died because of flooding and flood-related disaster is on the hands of those who took the people’s money.

Open Table Metropolitan Community Church, as a progressive, ecumenical, and LGBTQIA+ affirming Christian community, joins our outrage with every Filipino angry against corruption and corrupt politicians.

Our rage is further fueled by their blatant lying and denials, as well as the selective purge and performative outrage of this current administration, which does not seem to have any plans to investigate the government as a whole.

There are no sufficient words to express our indignation and rage against the shameless and demonic actions of those involved in corruption, not just with flood control but across different agencies, branches, and programs of the government.

This is even worse for those of us who have been personally and directly affected by floods. Some may even experience adverse physical manifestations of these emotions, such as physical exhaustion, body pains, or flu-like symptoms.
Our hearts, minds, and even our souls are having a whirlwind of mixed emotions and feelings of rage, exasperation, hopelessness, and anxiety.
The past several weeks, and indeed the last couple of days, have been emotionally and mentally challenging with all the revelations and allegations being exposed.
stole unimaginable amounts of taxpayers’ money intended for flood control and mitigation. They did this year after year while their people suffered.

killing lives, destroying properties, displacing communities, and adversely affecting our economy. And despite everything, politicians and other government officials, together with their private contractor accomplices,

CORRUPTION IN THE PHILIPPINE GOVERNMENT

Due to climate change and poor urban planning, not just in Metro Manila but in many other places in the country, flooding and flooding-related catastrophes have been worsening over the years,

After much prayer and discernment, the current interim board decided that it is time for the church to officially participate in protest mobilizations against social justice issues as part of the wider ecumenical network and justice movement.
Thus, earlier participation in protest rallies was an individual decision of our leaders and members.

The church remains a safe space for all people of different political leanings. We were also navigating how our progressive theological line will not be construed as politically endorsing any specific party, group, or personality.

The church has always been progressive. We have consistently spoken against social justice issues in our country and the world. In relation to protest rallies, we have been sensitive and careful with members who may have different socio-political views and persuasions.

Corruption is part of the larger social evil of injustice and oppression.

In previous years, only Pastor Joseph and a few members and leaders attended protest rallies like Labor Day and People’s SONA.

Nonetheless, it is our Christian duty to protest and denounce graft and corruption in our country and wherever and whenever it occurs. Inspired by the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets of old, our faith demands that we voice out our condemnation of corruption.

The church, however, will remain politically unaffiliated and unassociated, which means: (1) We will not be part of any political party. (2) We will not endorse any political party. (3) We will not endorse any political personality for any government position.
On this date the church is supposed to hold our 19th anniversary celebration and for this year we will honor our anniversary by participating in the protest rally in Luneta.

For the first time in its 19-year history, Open Table MCC's interim board has unanimously decided to officially join a protest rally against corruption happening in Luneta Park on the 21st of September, 2025.

May the light of the Risen Christ shine upon his servant, Francis the Brave. And may he forever share in God’s eternal joy.

-Rev. Joseph San Jose
Pastor, Open Table MCC

May the Roman Catholic faithful carry forward in their lives, parishes, religious communities, and dioceses the example and words of Pope Francis—words that reflect the heart of Jesus Christ, who welcomes and loves all.

As the conclave begins and the cardinals of the Roman Church prepare to elect a new pope, we pray for a fresh breath of the Holy Spirit to inspire them. May God bless the Church with a progressive new pope who will continue and expand the work of reform, compassion, and inclusion that Francis began.

We give thanks for his work within the Roman Church, his commitment to justice and peace, and his words and actions of compassion—all of which will continue to ripple throughout our diverse human family and into history.

Though Open Table MCC, as part of the global Metropolitan Community Church denomination, is not affiliated with the Roman Catholic Church, we join in prayer and mourning for this brave reformer and compassionate Pope.
Imperfect and a product of his own time, Pope Francis nevertheless showed us what it means to be the hands, feet, and voice of Christ in our troubled world today.

to care for the poor and the oppressed, to stand against injustice, to welcome refugees, to build friendships across religious, cultural, and other human divides, to uplift women’s voices, to protect our common home, and to listen deeply and reform courageously.

He was also a tireless advocate for ecumenical and interfaith dialogue, recently stating that different religions are different paths to God.

He was truly the Pope the world needed for such a time as this—a time when he reminded all of us, not just Catholics,

He spoke urgently about the need to care for creation and address climate change as a critical issue facing all of humanity. In one of his encyclicals, he criticized capitalism and the greed of those who profit from the destruction of the earth and its people.

Yet he did not mince words in criticizing the curia and its cardinals, particularly those aligned with traditionalist and conservative views.

Early in his papacy, Pope Francis condemned the violence in Syria and called on Christians to welcome refugees fleeing war and devastation.
he angered Roman Catholic conservatives by offering divorced and remarried Catholics to once again receive communion—prompting four senior cardinals to issue a letter of dubia challenging him.

He repeatedly expressed the need for greater inclusion of women in Church leadership, even appointing women religious to Vatican offices traditionally held by Cardinals and Bishops.

In addition to advocating for pastoral care and compassion for LGBTQIA+ people,

through a greater practice of synodality and standing against clerical and hierarchical abuse. He often spoke of the Church as a hospital for the sick and the hurting, not a refuge for the perfect and self-righteous. His simplicity extended to simplifying Church structures and liturgical practices.

This stands in contrast to his predecessors, who rarely spoke of LGBTQIA+ people with genuine compassion, if at all.

Taking the name of Francis, Jorge Cardinal Bergoglio signaled his intent to lead a papacy rooted in reform—decentering and democratizing the Church
with an affirmation of the union or a Church-recognized marriage. It is a blessing rooted in pastoral care, similar to blessings given to individuals, friends, groups, objects, or places.)

In the final year of his pontificate, he also approved the pastoral blessing of same-sex couples.*

(*The pastoral blessing for same-sex couples, as defined and clarified by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, is not a blessing of the relationship itself and should not be confused

He met and spoke with gay and trans individuals on several occasions. He will always be remembered by the queer community for saying, “Who am I to judge?” and for declaring that every gay child deserves a family and should never be thrown out.

While Pope Francis did not change any official church doctrine regarding LGBTQIA+ people—and at times used phrases like “gender ideology”—his courageous openness in addressing the LGBTQIA+ community, even using terms like “gay” or “LGBT,” was both unprecedented and remarkable.

As an ecumenical Christian church composed mostly of LGBTQIA+ Filipinos, we stand in prayer and solidarity with the Roman Catholic faithful in mourning the passing—and celebrating the life—of Pope Francis, the beloved reformer pope, who returned to God on the morning of April 21, 2025.
The Brave Pope of Compassion: A Statement of Solidarity with the Passing of Pope Francis - By Rev. Joseph San Jose
